extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; students of intellectual history and philosophy; thinkers evaluating aims of knowledge
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging philosophical systems with emphasis on their aims, methods, and social effects — especially the contrast between Platonic/ancient and Baconian approaches. Focus is on whether a philosophy advances human wellbeing, progress, and useful knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy's object: the good of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of philosophy should be 'the good of mankind' — to improve the human condition rather than to pursue mere abstract or inane speculation (Baconian aim: 'instaurationem philosophiae ejusmodi quae nihil inanis aut abstracti habeat, quaeque vitae humanae conditiones in melius provehat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a philosophical system by whether it tends to increase comforts, reduce suffering, extend human power over matter, and produce tangible benefits for ordinary people; contrast this with systems that exalt abstract ends divorced from human wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility over abstract speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural and moral speculation should be cultivated primarily for increasing the power and ameliorating the condition of man, not merely as intellectual exercises detached from use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating natural philosophy as 'merely a mental exercise' or subsidiary to disputation (Seneca example). Prefer work that yields practical discoveries and improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of truth and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should lead to accumulation of truth across generations rather than repeating the same disputations without harvest ('no accumulation of truth, no heritage of truth ... the garners contained only smut and stubble').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a school builds on predecessors to produce progressive additions to knowledge and technique, rather than cyclical, sterile argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding barren verbosity; emphasis on fruitful results
rubrics_metrics.description: The history of ancient schools shows 'words, and more words, and nothing but words' — philosophers must avoid sterile verbosity and produce usable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score negatively philosophies whose output is primarily rhetorical, declamatory, or subtle disputation without concrete results; reward those producing inventions, remedies, or usable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical cultivation of natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural philosophy should be cultivated with the intent to assuage suffering, multiply conveniences, extend human dominion over the material world, not merely to 'raise the mind above low cares.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer lines of inquiry aimed at technological, medical, agricultural, navigational, and similar applications; reject pursuits solely for abstruse intellectual exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing inventors and applied arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions (e.g., gunpowder, printing) and applied mechanics are of greater social value than scholastic learning that confers reputation but no practical advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging intellectual culture, weigh contributions to material progress (inventions, tools, processes) more heavily than erudition or rhetorical prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive empiricism: observation over authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy philosophical movement weakens 'blind reverence for authority' and values empirical inquiry and experiment over unreasoning submission to classical names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria: openness to varied sources, willingness to question received authorities (Aristotle), and adoption of methods that privilege observation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance before style
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid giving 'undue importance to the mere graces of style' — reformation of manner is inadequate if unaccompanied by reform in philosophical method and substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: valuing Latinity or polished diction (Aschams and Buchanans) more than corrective changes in how knowledge is sought and used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as an auxiliary, not an end
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical sciences should be regarded as the 'handmaid of natural philosophy' — useful insofar as they serve physical inquiry, not as superior for their own abstract discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematics by its contribution to empirical sciences and useful technologies rather than by claims to lead to abstract 'pure' truth divorced from application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living astronomy: explain influences and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomy should be 'living' — setting forth the nature, motion, and influences of heavenly bodies as they really are, not as remote exercises in abstract contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer astronomical inquiry that informs navigation, seasons, and physical causes over purely idealized, contemplative schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and record as instruments of advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing (alphabetical record) and external memory are useful tools to advance science and are to be valued for their instrumental role despite Plato's misgivings about dependence on written aids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge practices that improve collective memory, communication, and accumulation of results (books, records) as positive for progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicine valued for relieving suffering and prolonging life
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of medicine should be pursued to make imperfect men comfortable and to mitigate pain and disease — practical beneficence is a mark of a commendable discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor medical research and practice that yields cures, palliative methods, and improvements in wellbeing rather than theoretic pronouncements that treat extended life as undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation aimed at citizens' wellbeing (not moralizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of legislation is that 'cives feliciter degant' — the wellbeing and happiness of the people (through education, defence, order, justice, wealth), rather than only making men virtuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess laws by their capacity to secure prosperity, order, and protection; critique legal frameworks that prioritize rhetorical exhortation over practical provisions that secure citizens' welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and directness in legal form; avoid prologues
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should be direct and avoid long preambles ('Quantum fieri potest prologi evitentur, et lex incipiat a jussione').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a drafting standard, prefer concise commands and sanctions rather than lengthy discursive prefaces that 'introducunt disputantes non jubentes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for attainable, earth-bound goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer philosophical aims that are attainable and earth-bound ('Bacon fixed his eye on a mark which was placed on the earth, and within bow-shot, and hit it in the white') rather than lofty, impracticable ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward proposals and systems that deliver incremental, demonstrable improvements over those promising grand but unattainable transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-sense orientation and sympathy with popular notions
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophy grounded in common sense and sympathy with ordinary human desires (life, health, comfort, honour) is praiseworthy; avoid cant and illusion detached from everyday needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess thinkers by their realism about human motives and by the absence of pretentious abstractions that ignore the 'vulgar wants' of most people.
